t.11.1: Aṣṭāvakra said: He who is certain that existence, non-existence and change arise from the very nature of things becomes changeless and free from affliction, and easily attains peace.
t.11.2: He who is firmly convinced that Īśvara is the maker of all and that there are no others here has all his inner desires dissolved; at peace, he clings to nothing anywhere.
t.11.3: He who is certain that misfortunes and fortunes come in their due time from destiny alone is ever content, his senses at rest; he neither desires nor grieves.
t.11.5: Sorrow arises from anxious thought and in no other way here; one who is firmly convinced of this, freed from it, is happy and at peace, his desires everywhere fallen away.
t.11.4: He who is firmly convinced that pleasure and pain, birth and death come from destiny alone, who merely looks upon what is to be accomplished and is free from strain, is not tainted even while acting.
t.11.6: He who is firmly convinced, "I am not the body, nor is the body mine; I am pure awareness," has, as it were, attained kaivalya, and no longer remembers what he has done or left undone.
t.11.7: He who is firmly convinced, "From Brahmā down to a tuft of grass, I alone am all this," becomes free of mental constructions, pure and at peace, indifferent to what is gained and what is not gained.
t.11.8: One who is firmly convinced that this universe, a manifold wonder, is nothing at all becomes free of latent desires and is pure awareness alone; he is at peace, as though nothing existed.
